core: Individual needs assessment as a structured, collaborative, ongoing process whose product is a service plan
Assessment distinguished from diagnosis and from eligibility screening
Reassessment: why assessment is ongoing and what triggers a return to it
Sources of information (the person, collateral contacts, records, observation, specialized evaluations) and how to weigh them
Presenting problem vs underlying need vs the person's own stated priorities
Strengths, protective factors, and natural supports as assessment content rather than an afterthought
Risk and safety screening as a distinct strand with its own thresholds and timelines
What a standardized screening score does and does not establish, including positive predictive value reasoning
Cultural and linguistic factors in the validity of an assessment
Documentation: separating observation from inference, plain language, the person's own words
Turning assessment into a service plan with individually identified goals
Individual needs assessment contrasted with community health needs assessment
supporting: Assessment domains named in professional case management standards
Congruence between the person's goals and the program's structure and philosophy
Regulatory reassessment cadence under Medicaid home and community-based services rules
Weak predictive performance of suicide risk factors, and what that implies about the purpose of risk screening

claims.claim: Professional case management standards define assessment as engaging the client, and where appropriate other members of the client system, in an ongoing information-gathering and decision-making process that helps clients identify their own goals, strengths, and challenges, and state explicitly that assessment is an ongoing activity rather than a one-time event.

Under Medicaid home and community-based services rules, the evaluation of need for an institutional level of care is a separate, yes-or-no eligibility determination (reevaluated at least annually), while the written person-centered service plan must reflect clinical and support needs identified through an assessment of functional need.

Federal rules require the person-centered service plan to be reviewed, and revised as appropriate, based on a reassessment of functional need at least every 12 months, when the individual's circumstances or needs change significantly, or at the individual's request.

Federal child welfare guidance identifies the information streams that feed a comprehensive family assessment: review of existing records and prior service-system history, information from the reporter and collateral contacts, direct contact with the family, completed safety and risk assessments, observations of the home and of interactions, and specialized evaluations.

A comprehensive assessment focuses not only on presenting issues at a particular time but on the underlying causal factors behind behaviors and conditions, and is described as seeking the whole picture rather than a set of symptoms.

Case management standards direct the worker to support the client in establishing priorities and goals after discussing needs and strengths, and to attend to congruence between the client's goals and expectations and the structure and philosophy of the program, demonstrating flexibility, advocacy, or referral elsewhere where they do not fit.

Strengths and resources are assessment content: professional standards list psychosocial strengths, protective factors and points of resilience, relationships with community organizations and social supports, and past strategies among assessment domains; federal rules require the written service plan to reflect the individual's strengths and preferences and to name paid and unpaid supports including natural supports; and federal child welfare guidance directs that protective factors be used as points of leverage in the plan rather than recorded as a list of family characteristics.

Safety and risk assessment is a distinct strand: federal child welfare guidance distinguishes assessments of safety, risk, and special needs from comprehensive family assessment, states that comprehensive assessment builds on rather than substitutes for them, and notes that significant new information may trigger concurrent safety and risk assessment.

A meta-analysis of 365 studies spanning 50 years found that prediction of suicidal thoughts and behaviors from risk factors was only slightly better than chance across odds ratio, hazard ratio, and diagnostic accuracy analyses, that no broad category or subcategory predicted far above chance, and that predictive ability had not improved over the period.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force's 2023 recommendation on depression and suicide risk screening in adults states that all positive screening results should lead to additional assessment to confirm the diagnosis, determine symptom severity, and identify comorbid problems, and that adequate systems and staff are needed for benefit to follow; it gives depression screening a B grade and finds evidence insufficient (I) for suicide risk screening in these populations.

In an individual participant data meta-analysis of the PHQ-9 (58 studies, n=17,357), combined sensitivity and specificity were maximized at the standard cutoff of 10 or above among studies using semistructured diagnostic interviews (29 studies, 6,725 participants): sensitivity 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.92), specificity 0.85 (0.82 to 0.88). At the 14% prevalence observed in those data, positive predictive value would be about 49%, meaning roughly 51% of positive screens would be false positives.

The PHQ-9 item on thoughts of death and self-harm does not query suicidality specifically; in four studies in non-psychiatric settings, of participants endorsing that item only 18% to 35% reported suicidal thoughts on questions designed to assess suicide risk and only 3% to 20% reported a plan.

Case management standards treat standardized instruments as starting points for developing and refining an individualized, comprehensive assessment, and direct that when used they be explained clearly so the client understands what is being sought and how it will be used.

Cultural and linguistic factors are assessment content and affect what an assessment actually collects: federal child welfare guidance names the need to assess the cultural, ethnic, linguistic, and other individual factors influencing perception of needs; case management standards list language preference and proficiency, preferred methods of communication, and levels of literacy among assessment domains and direct workers to begin with cultural self-examination; the CLAS standards require language assistance at no cost, notice of its availability, and verified competence with untrained individuals and minors discouraged as interpreters; interpreter standards require complete rendering without addition, omission, or substitution; and federal rules require the planning process to reflect cultural considerations and be conducted in plain, accessible language for people with disabilities and limited English proficiency.

Assessment records are read by other providers, payers and utilization reviewers, and potentially in legal review, should carry the client's own words, stories, goals, and feedback, should be written in jargon-free language families can understand and be available in the family's language; and the written service plan itself must be understandable to the individual and written in plain language.

Keeping observation visibly separate from inference on the page is a practice discipline that follows from who reads the record; it is presented in the lesson as standard teaching justified by the documented range of readers and the plain-language requirements, not as a rule quoted from a single standard.

Federal rules describe the assessment-to-plan handoff in detail: the individual leads the person-centered planning process and it includes people they choose; the written plan must reflect strengths and preferences, include individually identified goals and desired outcomes, name paid and unpaid supports including natural supports, reflect risk factors and the measures in place to minimize them including back-up plans, identify who monitors the plan, and be finalized with the individual's informed consent.

Case management standards require service plans to be based on meaningful assessments and to carry specific, attainable, measurable objectives that the client helped prioritize; federal child welfare guidance adds that collecting and organizing assessment information is not an end in itself and that the move from information to the plan should be transparent to the family.

A community health needs assessment is a distinct, population-level activity: tax-exempt hospital facilities must, in a three-year cycle, define the community served, identify and prioritize significant health needs, identify resources potentially available to address them, take input from a governmental public health department and from members or representatives of medically underserved, low-income, and minority populations, adopt a written CHNA report, and make it widely available to the public, with an implementation strategy adopted separately.
In the United States the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline can be reached by call, by text, or by online chat, at any hour.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether screening for a condition is worth doing at all, given false positive rates
positions: The USPSTF recommends screening adults for major depressive disorder (grade B) where systems exist to diagnose, treat, or refer, and finds evidence insufficient for suicide risk screening in the same populations (grade I).

The PHQ-9 accuracy meta-analysis emphasizes that at the standard cutoff roughly half of positive screens in its dataset would be false positives, and notes that national guidelines in Canada and the UK differ from the U.S. position.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not adjudicate whether to screen. It teaches only what a positive result licenses: further assessment, not a finding. The USPSTF grades are reported as given, including the insufficient-evidence grade for suicide risk screening, so the lesson never implies screening is settled practice.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much a risk instrument can tell a practitioner about an individual
positions: Risk domains appear in professional assessment standards as content practitioners are expected to cover.

Fifty years of longitudinal research yields prediction only slightly better than chance, and item-level indicators such as the PHQ-9 death and self-harm item correspond poorly to suicidality when checked against purpose-built questions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are stated. The lesson frames risk screening as a trigger for response, review, and support under agency policy and supervision, rather than as forecasting, and does not give thresholds or procedures.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted that needs assessment is 'a foundational concept' students use 'to organize information' with no practice content, no distinction from diagnosis or eligibility, and no sources; none of it was verifiable because none of it was about anything specific.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms with circular definitions and no connection to assessment practice.
The draft's analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') and worked example ('a student reads a short scenario') carried no discipline content and were discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with sourced practice content: the ongoing-process definition from professional standards, the assessment/diagnosis/eligibility split anchored in Medicaid HCBS rules, the information-source list from federal child welfare guidance, and the screening-score reasoning anchored in the USPSTF recommendation and the PHQ-9 meta-analysis.
Added the explicit contrast with community health needs assessment, since the shared name is the main source of student confusion and the community version belongs to a different unit.
Added an explicit educational-material statement and removed anything that could function as a screening or risk protocol.
Recomputed the positive predictive value example independently rather than repeating a number, and confirmed it reproduces the figure published in the source (about 49%).
rightsIssues: The NASW Standards for Social Work Case Management (2013) are copyrighted, all rights reserved. Read via local PDF text extraction; every standard and interpretation used here is restated in original wording and no NASW text is reproduced.

The PHQ-9 accuracy meta-analysis is CC BY-NC 4.0. Only reported statistics are used, with attribution; no prose adapted. The PHQ-9 instrument itself is not reproduced, described item by item, or scored in this lesson.
The PHQ-8/PHQ-9 equivalency paper is an author manuscript deposited in PMC without an open licence; only its reported figures are cited, with attribution.

U.S. federal regulations (42 CFR 441.301, 42 CFR 441.302, 26 CFR 1.501(r)-3) and USPSTF recommendation statements are U.S. government works and not subject to domestic copyright; requirements are nevertheless restated rather than quoted at length.
The CLAS standards and the NCIHC interpreter standards carry no verified reuse licence and are treated as reference only.
No instrument, cutoff table, risk protocol, or assessment form is reproduced anywhere in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: NASW Standards for Social Work Case Management (2013)
sourceRecords.notes: Read in full via local PDF text extraction. Primary source for this lesson. Standard 5 (Assessment) supplies the definition used throughout: an ongoing information-gathering and decision-making process engaging clients and, where appropriate, other members of the client system, to help clients identify their goals, strengths, and challenges; the interpretation states that assessment is an ongoing activity and not a one-time event, describes reassessment as revisiting needs, assets, and priorities while serving monitoring and evaluative functions, treats standardized instruments as starting points that should be explained clearly to the client, lists the assessment domains (including home safety, language preference and proficiency, preferred communication and learning methods, literacy, cultural values, psychosocial strengths and protective factors, risk of suicide or homicide, risk of abuse, neglect or exploitation, past strategies, and the client's own perceptions of needed change), and directs attention to congruence between the client's goals and the program's structure and philosophy. Standard 6 supplies the service-planning requirements (plans based on meaningful assessments, specific, attainable, measurable objectives, client involvement in prioritizing). Standard 10 supplies record-keeping (continuity between providers, reimbursement, utilization review, support in the event of legal review, and the direction to incorporate clients' own words, stories, goals, and feedback). Standard 4 supplies the cultural and linguistic material. Copyright (c) 2013 NASW, all rights reserved; restated in original wording only.

sourceRecords.title: Comprehensive Family Assessment Guidelines for Child Welfare
sourceRecords.provider: Children's Bureau, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2005)
sourceRecords.notes: Federal practice guidance, 58 pages, re-downloaded and text-extracted for this topic. Supports: the list of information streams feeding a comprehensive assessment (records and prior service-system history; the reporter and collateral contacts; contacts with the family; completed safety assessments, safety plans, and risk assessments; observations of the home and of interactions; specialized evaluations); the distinction between assessments of safety, risk, and special needs and comprehensive family assessment, with comprehensive assessment building on rather than substituting for them and new information triggering concurrent safety and risk assessment; the focus on underlying causal factors rather than presenting issues alone and the 'big picture, not just a set of symptoms' framing; identification of strengths and protective factors as a named component and their use as points of leverage in the plan rather than a list of family characteristics; the foundations of quality practice (engagement, essential involvement of families and youth in identifying their own needs and strengths, and assessment of cultural, ethnic, linguistic, and other individual factors influencing perception of needs); the statement that collecting and organizing assessment information is not an end in itself and that the move to a service plan should be transparent to the family; ongoing assessment and updating as circumstances change; and documentation written in jargon-free language families can understand and available in the family's language. No licence statement on the PDF; wording is original throughout.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR 441.301 - Contents of request for a waiver (person-centered planning process and person-centered service plan)
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Federal Register / Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, via eCFR
sourceRecords.notes: Current text retrieved through the eCFR renderer API. Paragraph (c)(1) supports the person-centered planning process requirements: the individual leads the process, it includes people chosen by the individual, provides information and support so the individual can direct it and make informed choices, is timely and convenient, and reflects cultural considerations while being conducted in plain language accessible to people with disabilities and people with limited English proficiency. Paragraph (c)(2) supports the written plan requirements used in the lesson: reflect the individual's strengths and preferences; reflect clinical and support needs identified through an assessment of functional need; include individually identified goals and desired outcomes; reflect paid and unpaid supports including natural supports; reflect risk factors and measures in place to minimize them, including individualized back-up plans; be understandable to the individual, in plain language; identify who monitors the plan; and be finalized with informed consent. Paragraph (c)(3)(i) supports the reassessment cadence: review and revision at least every 12 months based on reassessment of functional need, on significant change in circumstances or needs, or at the individual's request.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR 441.302 - State assurances (evaluation of need for level of care)
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Federal Register / Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, via eCFR
sourceRecords.notes: Current text retrieved through the eCFR renderer API. Paragraph (c) supports the eligibility-screening contrast used in the lesson: 'evaluation' is defined as a review of an individual beneficiary's condition to determine whether the beneficiary requires the level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities, and whether, but for waiver services, they would otherwise be institutionalized; paragraph (c)(2) requires reevaluations at least annually. Used only to show that this is a yes-or-no program-entry determination distinct from the assessment of functional need behind the service plan. The lesson gives no eligibility advice for any program.

sourceRecords.title: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (Final Recommendation Statement, June 20, 2023)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the central screening-versus-diagnosis point: all positive screening results should lead to additional assessment to confirm the diagnosis, determine symptom severity, and identify comorbid psychological problems; benefit depends on adequate systems and clinical staff so that people who screen positive are appropriately diagnosed and treated or referred. Grade B for screening adults, including pregnant and postpartum persons and older adults, for major depressive disorder; Grade I (insufficient evidence) for screening for suicide risk in the same populations. Applies to adults who do not have a diagnosed mental health disorder or recognizable signs or symptoms. Reported as a recommendation and its grades, not as instruction to screen anyone.

sourceRecords.title: Accuracy of Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) for screening to detect major depression: individual participant data meta-analysis
sourceRecords.provider: Levis B, Benedetti A, Thombs BD, for the DEPRESsion Screening Data (DEPRESSD) Collaboration; BMJ 2019;365:l1476
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on PMC and figures verified against the abstract, results, and discussion sections rather than a summary. Data from 58 of 72 eligible studies (n=17,357; 2,312 major depression cases). Combined sensitivity and specificity maximized at cutoff 10 or above among the 29 studies using a semistructured reference interview (6,725 participants): sensitivity 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.92), specificity 0.85 (0.82 to 0.88). The discussion states that at the 14% prevalence in those data the positive predictive value would be only 49%, so 51% of positive screens would be false positives. The lesson's worked example recomputes this from the reported sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence and reproduces 48.9%. Only reported statistics are used; no prose adapted and the instrument itself is not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Equivalency of the diagnostic accuracy of the PHQ-8 and PHQ-9: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis
sourceRecords.provider: Wu Y, Levis B, Riehm KE, et al.; Psychological Medicine 2020;50(8):1368-1380 (author manuscript on PMC)
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on PMC. Supports the point that an individual item on a symptom scale is not a risk assessment: the PHQ-9 item asks about thoughts of being better off dead or of hurting oneself and does not query suicidality specifically; across four studies in non-psychiatric settings (veterans in primary care, coronary artery disease patients, cancer patients), 7% to 21% of participants endorsed the item, but of those only 18% to 35% reported thoughts of suicide on questions designed specifically to assess suicide risk and only 3% to 20% reported a plan. Author manuscript deposited in PMC with no open licence; only reported figures cited.

sourceRecords.title: Risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors: A meta-analysis of 50 years of research
sourceRecords.provider: Franklin JC, Ribeiro JD, Fox KR, et al.; Psychological Bulletin 2017;143(2):187-232 (doi 10.1037/bul0000084; PMID 27841450)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record and full abstract retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API (the article itself is paywalled). Supports the limits of risk prediction: random-effects meta-analysis of 365 studies and 3,428 risk factor effect sizes over 50 years found that across odds ratio, hazard ratio, and diagnostic accuracy analyses prediction was only slightly better than chance for all outcomes, no broad category or subcategory predicted far above chance, and predictive ability had not improved across 50 years. Used in the lesson only to establish that risk screening triggers response and review rather than forecasting outcomes; no risk factors, thresholds, or procedures are reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 26 CFR 1.501(r)-3 - Community health needs assessments
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Federal Register / Internal Revenue Service, via eCFR
sourceRecords.notes: Current text retrieved through the eCFR renderer API. Used solely for the contrast between individual and community needs assessment. Supports: a hospital facility must have conducted a CHNA in the taxable year or either of the two preceding years, and an authorized body must adopt an implementation strategy; the required steps are defining the community served, assessing its health needs, soliciting and taking into account input from persons representing the broad interests of the community, documenting the assessment in a written CHNA report adopted by an authorized body, and making that report widely available to the public; assessing community health needs means identifying significant health needs, prioritizing them, and identifying resources potentially available to address them; and required input sources include at least one governmental public health department (or State Office of Rural Health) and members of, or organizations representing, medically underserved, low-income, and minority populations. The lesson does not teach how to conduct a CHNA; that belongs to the community-practice topic.

sourceRecords.title: National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Health and Health Care
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health (Think Cultural Health)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record; URL matches the existing registry entry. Supports Standards 5 to 8 as applied to assessment: language assistance offered at no cost to the individual, notice that it is available, verification of the competence of those providing it with untrained individuals and minors avoided and discouraged as interpreters, and easy-to-understand materials. Used here for the point that an assessment conducted without competent language assistance has not collected what the record will claim it collected. Rights not separately verified on the page, so treated as reference only.

sourceRecords.title: National Standards of Practice for Interpreters in Health Care
sourceRecords.provider: National Council on Interpreting in Health Care
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record; URL matches the existing registry entry. Used narrowly for the accuracy standards - render all messages completely without adding, omitting, or substituting - which is the reason an ad hoc interpreter undermines the validity of assessment information rather than merely slowing the conversation.
